guard.oathbreak.newspaper.title: The Oath-Eaten Blade
guard.oathbreak.newspaper.caption: Illustration: the north gate at dusk.
guard.oathbreak.newspaper.body.before:
The north gate of Montor. Dusk.

Ser Titus stood with his greatsword resting point-down on the stone, both hands folded over the pommel. He had been standing at this gate for eight years. The same gate. The same hour. The same sword.

A rusted arrowhead was still wedged between two stones near the arch—left there after an orc raid four summers past. He had taken the chieftain's head that day and hung it from the battlements. Then he came back down and stood here.

The townsfolk called him the Iron Bolt. Children counted the scars on his pauldrons and made up stories about each one. No one—not the merchants who passed him at dawn, not the whores who waved from the upper windows, not Ser Titus himself—doubted one thing:

He had never fallen.

Not "never lost." Never fallen.

A true guard did not die. This was not a secret in the cities of Sosaria. It was a fact, like rain or rust. Every guard's breastplate bore the same mark: an open book pressed beneath a bare sword. Not decoration. A contract.

The Oath.

On the day of his investiture, each guard had his name driven into the foundation stone of the city he would serve. From that moment, he ceased to be a common man. The city poured its will into his blood—made him unkillable. His sword was no longer iron and edge. It was the city's reach made solid. Order given flesh.

When that blade fell, it did not merely cut. It judged.

This was why guards never stayed dead. Demons could breach the outer wall. The dead could crawl from the earth inside the chapel yard. But the guard would rise. Again. And again. The Oath saw to that.

The Oath also bound.

In the crypts beneath Montor's oldest quarter, sealed behind a door that no living man had opened, something older than the city's charter lay interred. A machine. A heart. It had been there since before the first stone of Montor was laid—since the days of the dark exodus, when the fleeing kings buried their engines beneath the earth and swore the cities into being with gears and blood.

The Oath was not a prayer. It was a mechanism. Every guard who stood at his post was a gear in that buried clockwork. The city's will was not a spirit. It was a current, flowing from that sunless chamber, through the foundation stone, into the blade.

Ser Titus did not know this. No guard did.

But the machine knew him.
guard.oathbreak.newspaper.body.after:
That night, five men sat at a corner table in Montor's Tap and Tread.

No one remembered them entering. No one noted their hoods. Had anyone traced the bounty sheet from Raven's Vale, they might have matched three of the faces. Of course, the men who could have made those matches were already dead.

"North gate. Three spans after the shift-change." The speaker pushed a scrap of parchment to the center of the table. A charcoal sketch of the gatehouse—proportions rough, but the angles were right. "Last time we tested him, I thought he was just healing."

"He was healing," another voice said.

"Yes. But also no." The speaker traced a line across the sketch with his finger. "On the third exchange, I felt it. His recovery lagged—maybe half a heartbeat. You would not see it if you were not inside his reach, inside his rhythm, waiting for it." He paused. "I counted. Twice he dropped. Twice he stood. But between the second fall and the rise, there was a flicker. Like oil wiped from a lamp-glass."

The third man spoke. His voice was low, ground like millstone grit. "He cannot die once. He can die three times. The third fall is the one that holds."

The table was quiet.

One of them—the youngest—shifted in his seat. "Then how do we survive three rounds with him?"

The third man looked at him. "We do not survive. We overlap. Three of us, one on each fall. Spread the breaking across three bodies. No single spine takes it all."

"You have done this before," the young one said.

It was not a question.

The third man's hand moved to his belt, where a tool hung—a thing of black iron and crystal, curved like a question mark. He did not answer.

"Move."

Ser Titus saw them before they reached the gate.

A guard did not need to ask questions. He read the walk: men who had covered ground, men who had spilt blood. His thumb rubbed the leather wrap of his sword-grip once.

They came fast.

The first man carried a crescent axe—a sweeping blade that hooked past Titus's guard and bit into the gap between cuirass and pauldron. Titus twisted, drove his pommel into the man's temple, felt bone crack. But the second was already inside his reach, a short blade punching up into the back of his knee. Titus bellowed, slammed the second man away with his shield-boss, and felt the blood running down his leg in three separate streams.

He knew he was about to fall.

He also knew what that meant.

The Oath surged in him like a deep-water current. In the moment of collapse, the city would catch him. He would rise. Wounds undone. Breath restored. Fighting weight returned.

He fell.

The cobblestones hit his back. And in that instant, he heard—not with his ears—a low thrum beneath the world. The voice of the buried engine. The names of every guard who had ever stood, drilled into the stone.

NOT YET.

He stood.

Someone among the five cursed. But the axe-man did not hesitate. The second wave was already breaking.

The second fall came faster. Titus felt the rhythm falter. The Oath was still there, still pulling him up—but the pull was shallower. Like a well drawn too many times in a single hour. He heard his own armor groan.

He rose again.

His strength was a fraction thinner.

The axe-man's eyes caught the change. A hunter's light kindled there.

"Third," the man said. Not to his companions. To Titus.

The third rush was only three men.

But they were the right three.

Ser Titus's knee touched stone. And this time, the earth did not lift him.

The Oath was not infinite.

The city's will had promised him forever, but it had not promised forever spent in a single night. When a guardian was broken by the same enemies, in the same fury, three times within the turning of an hourglass, the covenant—stretched too fast, too hard—gave way.

Like an over-wound spring. Like a gear stripped of its teeth.

Deep beneath Montor, in the sealed crypt, a hairline crack ran across the surface of the buried engine. No one saw it. No one heard it. But the current stuttered.

Ser Titus looked up. The axe-man stood over him, iron boots a foot from his face.

"You—" Titus began. He did not know what he meant to say.

He never finished.

The breastplate's emblem—the book, the sword—made a sound like a frozen twig snapping.

His sword fell from his hand.

The axe-man—whose name, the bounty posters would read by morning, was Korn—stooped and took the blade.

It was heavier than it looked. No. That was not weight. That was warmth. The hilt was hot, as though fresh from the forge. He lifted it, and something vast and alien traveled up his arm and into his chest. Six hundred years of order. Law. The unbearable weight of a city watching itself.

He stared into the steel and saw, for an instant, Montor reflected—not its streets, but the shape of its will. Compressed. Hungry.

In that moment, Korn believed he could split a mountain.

His companion touched his shoulder. "Go."

Word traveled faster than they did. The fall of the north gate guard moved through Montor like fire through dry timber. Bells began to toll.

Korn ran into the dusk with the sword in his fist.

The first stroke caught a cavalry horse that blocked their path. The blade passed through the animal's chest and out the other side without slowing. The rider was thrown twelve feet. The force of it made Korn's teeth ache.

The second strike split a pursuer's shield—iron-bound, boss-riveted—like dry bread.

The third stroke left a hairline crack across the blade.

The fourth brought frost. Not on the air—on the steel. A web of silver fissures crawled from the edge toward the fuller. Korn felt the warmth draining out of the grip. The buried engine, far below, was withdrawing its gift.

Moonlight fell through the cracks. The blade was a lantern of broken glass.

One more. He knew it.

"It is dying," one of his companions said.

Korn nodded. He did not slow. He waited—not for the nearest enemy, but for the one that deserved it.

The fifth swing.

The blade met its target and shattered into a hundred silver shards, ringing off the cobblestones like a bell struck once and then dropped. Korn was left holding a hilt wrapped in leather and the memory of heat. Blood ran from his palm where the fragments had cut him.

Behind him, the bells of Montor still rang. Torches were being lit along the wall, one after another, a ripple of fire spreading through the dark. He knew his face would be on every notice board by sunrise. Guard-Slayer. Double-murder bounty. Wanted alive or dead—preferably dead.

He did not look back.

The fragments lay scattered across the street. Night wind tumbled them into the gutter.

— END —
